claims: Unilateral and bilateral landings have materially different knee kinematics and muscle-activation demands.
A lateral hurdle task must declare takeoff foot count, landing foot count and leg, obstacle, direction, contact count, terminal hold, and reset; hop or jump wording alone cannot supply those facts.
Bilateral and unilateral hurdle jumps showed different force and contact-time characteristics in a standardized protocol.

Raised-hurdle clearance is represented separately from a floor-line or open-floor target because it adds required equipment, minimum clearance, visual demand, trip exposure, and altered failure consequences.
Jump landing uses foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk control, with different demands when landing on one leg versus two.
Cards declare plantar flexors, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals, hip adductors and rotators, foot and ankle stabilizers, and trunk stabilizers without implying isolated-muscle causation.
Changing hurdle height altered jump height and flight-phase hip and knee positions in the studied hurdle-jump protocol.
The exact card fixes one lateral clearance, declared low obstacle dimensions, declared takeoff and landing support, controlled absorption, terminal hold, and full reset.
Hurdle and support conditions change mechanical and coordination demands and therefore must remain fixed when comparing tasks.
Difficulty scores exercise complexity and physical difficulty only, with overall derived as their maximum; athlete proficiency is not an exercise-card field.
Hurdle height can alter clearance strategy even when some lower-limb work measures do not differ between tested heights.

Track obstacle dimensions, bodyweight contacts, takeoff and landing support, direction, landing quality, attempts, other jump and running load, symptoms, rest, and recovery without asserting a universal threshold.
Obstacle dimensions are part of the task and cannot be treated as invisible equipment metadata.
Require a collapsible low hurdle, level high-traction surface, marked takeoff and landing zones, clear fall space, no cross-traffic, stable footwear policy, and a complete coach sightline.
Landing-feedback interventions use observable movement targets, but the evidence does not establish one universal safe repetition count.
Dose fully reset single clearances, count every landing contact and side, preserve the declared hold, and stop before technique or output changes.
Lateral line drills distinguish one-foot and two-foot execution and demonstrate why support must be named explicitly.
Instructions state foot support, direction, obstacle, takeoff zone, clearance, landing zone, whole-foot absorption, hold, exit, and reset.
Hurdle height changes flight posture and must be selected deliberately rather than progressed by assumption.

Stop for pain, guarding, obstacle contact, toe catch, uncontrolled landing, split or wrong-foot contact, free-foot touch, extra hop or step, target miss, alignment loss, dizziness, unsafe equipment, or two changed reps.
Bilateral and unilateral hurdle protocols have different mechanical characteristics and should not be pooled silently.

Workout generation validates exact card and variant, obstacle inventory and dimensions, lane, side balance, contact and fatigue budgets, duration, rest, substitutions, and persisted output after every change.
Clear observable landing feedback can support movement practice, but card text cannot promise injury prevention.
Athlete support explains the foot contract, obstacle, target, expected landing, symptoms, self-checks, stop rule, and how to request a ground-only or non-impact alternative.
Standardized hurdle protocols require the support condition and obstacle setup to remain consistent.
Coaches document hurdle dimensions, takeoff and landing marks, foot contract, direction, valid attempts, contacts, hold, rest, side order, faults, symptoms, and substitutions.
Changing from unilateral to bilateral landing changes the task rather than merely reducing difficulty.

Accessible delivery may reduce obstacle height, lateral distance, intent, attempts, precision, or measurement pressure and increase rest or multimodal instruction while preserving the exact support and obstacle contract.
Obstacle height is a meaningful mechanical dimension and must be bounded within the reviewed variant.

Support, landing leg, obstacle versus floor target, contact count, rebound, approach, rotation, and terminal action require explicit variant or definition review; measured distance, hold duration, attempts, and rest can be delivery modifiers within bounds.
YouTube oEmbed health establishes current link and embedding availability only.

A human must watch the full video and verify foot support, obstacle, direction, contact count, clearance, landing, hold, reset, cueing, safety, captions, accessibility, and demonstration quality before approval.
